Carthage

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
[Image: The circular military harbour of ancient Carthage, reconstructed from its surviving island admiralty]

Carthage was an ancient city in present-day Tunisia, founded by Phoenician settlers from Tyre — traditionally in 814 BC — which grew into the dominant commercial power of the western Mediterranean. From its superb twin harbours the Carthaginians traded from Iberia to Sicily, governed an empire of colonies and subject peoples, and fought Rome in the three Punic Wars (264–146 BC). Hannibal's invasion of Italy made Carthage Rome's most feared enemy; its defeat and total destruction in 146 BC became a byword for annihilation, though a Roman Carthage later rose on the site.

Republic and empire

Carthage was governed as a republic by two annually elected suffetes, a senate of wealthy families and popular assemblies, with powerful councils that Aristotle praised. Its wealth rested on agriculture in the fertile Tunisian hinterland, manufactures, and control of sea trade; its war fleets and mercenary armies defended colonies in Sicily, Sardinia, Corsica and Iberia. The city's religion worshipped Baal Hammon and Tanit; the tophet precinct, where urns of cremated infants were buried, remains fiercely debated by scholars.

The Punic Wars and destruction

Rome and Carthage clashed over Sicily in 264 BC; Carthage lost the First Punic War and Sicily, then built a new Iberian empire under the Barcid family. Hannibal's march over the Alps (218 BC) opened the Second Punic War; after fifteen years of war in Italy he was recalled and defeated at Zama (202 BC). A humbled Carthage recovered commercially, but Rome, urged on by Cato the Elder's cry that 'Carthage must be destroyed', provoked the Third Punic War (149–146 BC): after a two-year siege the city was stormed, its population enslaved and its buildings razed.
